findings.title: Date overrides bypass booking and calendar conflicts
findings.body: A slot inside a date override returns here before the `busy.every` check. An override should make the host available outside their normal hours, but it should not make existing bookings or calendar events disappear. As a result, getSchedule can advertise slots that conflict with a host's existing commitments, risking double bookings.

findings.title: Multiple override windows on one date reject each other's slots
findings.body: The find callback returns true when a slot is outside an individual override, and find stops at the first true result. If a user has two separate override windows on the same date, a slot in either window is outside the other one and gets rejected before the matching window can be considered. Valid slots in multi-window date overrides are therefore hidden.

findings.title: Working-hours validation does not check that one window contains the full slot
findings.body: The validator sets end to the slot start instead of slot start plus eventLength, so a slot can be accepted even when the event runs past a host's working-hours end. It also returns an invalid result when the slot is outside any one same-day window, rather than checking whether some window contains it; users with split working hours can have valid slots rejected. In round-robin events, candidates from another host's availability can consequently be offered even when the fixed host cannot host the full event.

findings.title: Timezone conversion drops date changes when an override crosses midnight
findings.body: Adding the timezone offset can move the converted override to a different calendar day, but this code keeps only its hour and minute. The active-override selection still uses the original date, so the converted time is then placed on the wrong invitee day. For example, a 00:30 override in UTC+10 converted for a UTC invitee belongs to the previous day at 14:30, but the code selects it on the original day and places it at 14:30 there.

findings.title: The start-time offset is reused for the override end across DST changes
findings.body: The offset is calculated once from override.start and applied to override.end as well. If the override spans a daylight-saving transition, the organizer's offset can differ at the two endpoints, shifting the end time by an hour. For example, a New York override from 01:00 to 04:00 on the spring-forward day should end at 08:00 UTC for a UTC invitee, but reusing the start offset can extend it to 09:00 UTC and expose an extra hour.

findings.title: The added test does not cover the fixed-host round-robin behavior
findings.body: The new test changes the timezone for a personal event, but its scenario has no round-robin scheduling type or fixed hosts. It therefore does not exercise the primary claimed fix: filtering round-robin slots using a fixed host's date override. A regression in that path would not be caught by this test.
